question: Horses \(X,\) \(Y,\) and \(Z\) are entered in a three-horse race in which ties are not possible. If the odds against \(X\) winning are \(3\)-to-\(1\) and the odds against \(Y\) winning are \(2\)-to-\(3,\) what are the odds against \(Z\) winning? (By “odds against \(H\) winning are \(p\)-to-\(q\)” we mean that the probability of \(H\) winning the race is \(\frac{q}{p+q}.\))
solution:
Write \(P(X)\) for the probability that \(X\) wins, and similarly for the other horses. The given definition of odds gives
\[
P(X)=\frac{1}{3+1}=\frac14,
\qquad
P(Y)=\frac{3}{2+3}=\frac35.
\]
Because there are three horses and no ties, exactly one of these three winning events occurs. Thus
\[
P(Z)=1-\frac14-\frac35
=\frac{20-5-12}{20}
=\frac3{20}.
\]
The probability that \(Z\) does not win is therefore \(17/20\). Odds against winning compare the probability of not winning with the probability of winning, so the required ratio is
\[
\frac{17}{20}:\frac3{20}=17:3.
\]
The odds against \(Z\) winning are \(17\)-to-\(3\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
